title: Generating Voice from Text Using Local Models

slides.title: Intro
slides.transcript: [warmly] Generating Voice from Text Using Local Models. <break time="0.4s" /> By Hisham Abu ella. <break time="0.8s" /> I've been building a personal AI engine that runs entirely on my Mac Studio. Text was the first step. The natural next question was, can I generate voice locally too? [excited] It turns out, yes. And the results are surprisingly good. <break time="0.5s" /> When I first wrote this in February, local voice meant one model and one experiment. Since then, voice has become part of everyday projects. Bedtime stories for my son, narrated in my own voice. Local voice engines built into my AI engine. And a tool that renders a whole story locally or through ElevenLabs, from the same script. [playfully] And yes, this reading is my cloned voice too.

slides.title: Four Voices
slides.transcript: The same bedtime page, four voices. <break time="0.5s" /> The newest example is the goodnight page from Susu the Cat, the second of my son's bedtime books. Same script, four voices. One from ElevenLabs in the cloud, and three made locally on the Mac Studio. You can play them all on the page. <break time="0.4s" /> When I first made this comparison, only the cloud version sounded like me. [warmly] That has changed. The second version is my own voice, cloned on the Mac Studio, and it whispers where the script says whisper, just like ElevenLabs. <break time="0.4s" /> [curious] The other thing is timing. The two preset voices read the page more than fifty percent slower. That matters in a picture book, where the page shouldn't turn before the sentence ends. My local clone lands in between, at ten seconds against eight and a half.

slides.title: Eleven v4
slides.transcript: What changed at ElevenLabs. <break time="0.5s" /> The bedtime books are narrated with ElevenLabs version four, my default now. The big change from the older models is how you steer it. Older versions had dials, like stability and style. Version four ignores the style dial, and takes directions written into the script instead. Words like warmly, softly, or whispers, in brackets, plus exact pauses. <break time="0.4s" /> One recipe, stability at one half and similarity at point eight, produced a hundred and six clips across two bilingual books, first try, with nothing redone. It speaks eighty five languages, which matters for my Arabic projects. But it isn't reproducible. The same seed and text gave different audio twice, so keep the file you like. <break time="0.4s" /> [playfully] One pleasant surprise. On my account it used roughly a tenth of the quota the script length suggested, and the directions and pauses didn't seem to count at all. Your plan may differ, so measure first.

slides.title: Voicebox
slides.transcript: Local voices inside my AI engine. <break time="0.5s" /> In February I said the next step was building voice into my AI engine. That's done, through Voicebox, an open source voice studio that runs on Apple Silicon. My engine uses it both ways. Speech to text when I record a question on my phone, and text to speech when I want an answer read aloud. <break time="0.4s" /> It comes with several engines. Kokoro, with dozens of preset voices, for fast drafts. Kwen Custom Voice, which takes delivery directions in plain language. And a few cloning engines, Chatterbox and Tada among them, which can copy a voice from a short recording. <break time="0.4s" /> The catch for my projects is Arabic. None of the local engines ship an Arabic preset voice. Only the cloning engines speak it, so Arabic needs a clean recording to clone from. In the cloud, I just pick an Arabic voice.

slides.title: My Own Voice, Locally
slides.transcript: My own voice, locally. <break time="0.5s" /> Cloning my own voice was at the top of my list, so I held a bake off. I took the newest and most liked open source voice models, and gave each one the same short recording of my voice. Each one read the same bedtime book, and I ran every page back through speech to text, to count the words it got wrong. <break time="0.4s" /> [excited] The surprise was that every local model read the words as accurately as ElevenLabs. Accuracy no longer separates them. What does is whether it sounds like me, and whether it can follow delivery. Fish S two Pro won on both. It understands the same directions already in my scripts, so a line marked whisper for ElevenLabs is whispered locally too. <break time="0.4s" /> Two honest caveats. The license is non commercial, which is fine for my site and my son's books, but not for a product. And this first clone learned from about nineteen seconds of my ElevenLabs narration. A copy of a copy. A clean recording is the next step. <break time="0.4s" /> [warmly] I added it to Voicebox as a new engine, and made it the default voice in my AI engine. When I ask for an answer read aloud, it now comes back in my own voice.

slides.title: Egyptian Arabic, Locally
slides.transcript: Egyptian Arabic, locally. Not yet. <break time="0.5s" /> Every bedtime book also has an Egyptian Arabic edition, so I ran the same test in Egyptian. Two texts. The Egyptian edition of Bismillah, which ElevenLabs already narrates, and a new six page story I wrote for the test. Alongside the general models, I added the open models tuned for Egyptian that I could find, like VoiceTut, trained on about three hundred and eighty hours of Egyptian speech, and NileTTS. <break time="0.4s" /> [curious] This time the numbers are harder to read. Speech to text mishears Egyptian on its own, so even the ElevenLabs narration that ships in the book scores sixteen percent. Most local models land between fifteen and thirty percent, inside that noise. The clearest sign is Kwen three, which doesn't support Arabic at all, and still scores in the same band. <break time="0.4s" /> What the numbers can show is a voice that breaks. NileTTS swung from nineteen percent on one text to fifty six on the other. So the scores tell me which clips to throw away, not which voice to keep. [gently] I haven't judged the Egyptian voices by ear yet. Until I do, my Arabic narration stays with ElevenLabs.

slides.title: One Script, Two Backends
slides.transcript: One script, two backends. <break time="0.5s" /> The newest piece is a batch voice over tool. It takes the same script I use for ElevenLabs, one entry per page, and renders every page locally, with the same file names. The story player doesn't care which one made the audio. <break time="0.4s" /> Most local engines have never heard of a direction like warmly, and would read it out loud. So the tool removes the directions, splits the script at every pause, renders each piece, and stitches them back together with real silence. [gently] As the notes put it, pacing survives the move. Emotion does not. The exception is Fish S two Pro, which reads the directions instead of skipping them. <break time="0.4s" /> Afterwards it checks every clip for silence, truncation, or stretching. [excited] Stretching is the clever one. Garbled speech still plays as a perfectly valid file, but it takes far longer per character than its neighbours, so it stands out. <break time="0.5s" /> Draft locally for free, then spend cloud credits on the final cut. Same script, one command to switch.

slides.title: Lessons
slides.transcript: Lessons from the bedtime stories. <break time="0.5s" /> Text to speech falls apart on bare sound words. My first try at the animal sounds used strings like moo with ten o's, with the expression turned up, [laughs] and it came back warbling. Wrapping each one in a short sentence, like the cow says moo, fixed it completely. <break time="0.4s" /> Write for the ear. Spell out numbers, skip abbreviations, keep sentences short, one idea per page. Every script goes through a small checker before any audio is made. <break time="0.4s" /> And check the words, not just the file. For this article, I ran every local clip back through speech to text to confirm it said what the script said. The goodnight page came back word for word from all three voices. Now the new pipeline does that check by itself, one sentence at a time. If a sentence comes back wrong, it's made again, up to four times, and the best take is kept.

slides.title: The Podcast
slides.transcript: The podcast, then and now. <break time="0.5s" /> This is where the project started. In February I wrote a five minute podcast script about my AI engine, and generated it twice. Once locally with VibeVoice, and once with ElevenLabs, using a clone of my voice. In October I ran the exact same script through the two new local engines, so all four versions can be compared on the page. <break time="0.4s" /> [surprised] Kokoro is the surprise. It rendered the whole five minute episode in twenty six seconds, less time than it takes to listen to the first paragraph. Kwen Custom Voice took about nine minutes. Checked back through speech to text, both new versions matched the script about ninety eight percent word for word, and nearly every difference was spelling, not a misreading. <break time="0.4s" /> One thing to keep in mind. The script is from February, so it describes the project as it was then. I kept it unchanged on purpose, so every version reads the same words.

slides.title: VibeVoice
slides.transcript: What is VibeVoice? <break time="0.5s" /> VibeVoice is a long form, conversational text to speech model, first developed by Microsoft and now maintained by the open source community. It makes expressive, multi speaker audio from plain text. Podcast conversations, narration, even background music it decides to add on its own. It's still what I reach for when a script has more than one speaker. <break time="0.4s" /> Under the hood, a language model handles the text, while a diffusion model generates the fine detail of the sound. The result has natural pacing, intonation, and consistent speakers. It comes in three sizes, from a small real time model to a seven billion parameter model with the most realistic output. <break time="0.4s" /> With sixty four gigabytes of memory, I can comfortably run the largest one. A full podcast episode takes a few minutes. Not real time, but perfectly fine for making content. And all of it happens on my machine.

slides.title: Local vs Cloud
slides.transcript: Local versus cloud, eight months later. <break time="0.5s" /> I use ElevenLabs for anything that ships. The bilingual narration on my Islamic kids website, the Wireless one oh one podcasts, and the bedtime books. Local covers everything before that. <break time="0.4s" /> Local is free and unlimited, ideal for drafts. It's completely private. Kokoro renders a page in seconds, VibeVoice does multi speaker podcasts, and it's built right into my AI engine. And now it has my own voice, with emotional directions. On the other hand, most local engines still ignore those directions, Arabic works only by cloning, it reads slower, and the best clone is non commercial. <break time="0.4s" /> ElevenLabs has the best quality, and the clone sounds like me. It follows directions for whispering, warmth, and pauses, and has ready Arabic voices. [sighs] But it costs credits, the text goes to a third party, the same seed won't give the same audio, and it needs the internet. <break time="0.5s" /> [gently] The gap keeps closing. Local is now good enough to draft a whole book for free. For the first time, that includes my own voice. The cloud still earns its place on the final cut, and on Arabic.

slides.title: What's Next
slides.transcript: What's next. <break time="0.5s" /> In February the next step was voice input. That's done. I can record a question on my phone and have it transcribed locally. Cloning my own voice locally is done too. What's left is a proper recording to clone from, instead of my ElevenLabs narration. And Arabic narration locally. The Egyptian test narrowed it to a few candidates, but speech to text can't pick the winner, and I haven't judged them by ear yet. So for now, Arabic stays in the cloud. And more bedtime books. The series grows with my son, and each new one is another chance to see how far the local voices have come. <break time="0.5s" /> [warmly] The tools are here. The hardware is capable. The open source community keeps pushing the models forward. Running your own AI voice pipeline is no longer a research project. It's a weekend project.
